Description: Probabilistic classifier assuming continuous features follow a Gaussian distribution; applies Bayes’ theorem with independence assumption.
Pros: Very fast, works with small data; Handles continuous features; Outputs probability estimates; Robust to irrelevant features
Cons: Independence assumption often violated; Gaussian assumption may not hold; Weak with correlated features
Typical Use Cases: Medical data (blood pressure, cholesterol); Sensor data classification; Quick baseline on tabular datasets

Description: Probabilistic classifier assuming features are counts/frequencies (e.g., words in text).
Pros: Excellent for text classification; Handles high-dimensional sparse data; Simple & fast; Needs little data
Cons: Only works with non-negative count features; Ignores feature correlation; Ignores word order (bag-of-words)
Typical Use Cases: Spam detection; News/topic categorization; Sentiment analysis

Description: Extension of SVM to regression; fits a function within an ε-insensitive margin, focusing on support vectors.
Pros: Captures non-linear patterns via kernels; Robust to outliers (ε-insensitive loss); Effective on small/medium datasets
Cons: Sensitive to hyperparameters (C, ε, γ); Computationally heavy on large data; Harder to interpret
Typical Use Cases: Stock price prediction; Energy demand forecasting; Non-linear regression tasks

Description: Linear model estimating class probabilities using a logistic (sigmoid) function.
Pros: Simple, interpretable; Produces calibrated probabilities; Works with continuous & categorical features; Fast to train
Cons: Assumes linear boundaries; Weak on non-linear data; Sensitive to multicollinearity
Typical Use Cases: Binary classification (spam/ham, churn); Medical diagnosis; Credit risk scoring
